Danny D’Imperio

Drummer Danny D’Imperio has thrived in a variety of musical settings including classic jazz with the Salt City Six, big band with Woody Herman and Maynard Ferguson, and hard bop with his own group, The Bloviators. His recordings as a leader include “Glass Enclosure,” “Hip To It” and “Still Comin’ On Up” with The Metropolitan Bopera House.
Danny was interviewed in Cortland, New York, on June 30, 2014, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and I’m here for the Fillius Jazz Archive, in Cortland, New York with drummer and band leader Danny D’Imperio. Thanks for joining me.
My pleasure.
You and I are only a few years apart, and I have some vivid memories of what grabbed me as a kid musically, and I’m wondering what grabbed you?

Well first of all my father, who was that man there, was a musician. And I was born on March 14, 1945 in Sydney, New York, and we lived in Unadilla, New York. And he quit playing. At that time he was four years old, that was on the centerfold of the New York Times along with Crown Prince Hirohito, who was 16 years old. I’ve got the original newspaper upstairs. It’s just barely holding together. But he quit playing drums when he was about five. I mean you can see by those drums, I mean with that gooseneck hanging down. Actually it’s hard to see but there actually is a cymbal that’s attached to the bass drum pedal. They didn’t have high-hat cymbals in those days and so like when you hit the drum the cymbal would also hit the drum with the bass drum beater. I’d love to have that set of drums but I don’t know whatever happened to it. But anyway, he quit playing drums shortly thereafter. And around the age of 12 or 13 he contracted rheumatic fever and stayed home from school for one year as a result, and learned how to play the piano. So when I was born he worked for the War Department, he couldn’t get in the service at that time because of the rheumatic heart, so he worked for the War Department, and played piano on the side. So my first recollections when we lived in Unadilla, New York on the coffee table in the living room were the old 78 albums, which you open them up and there’d be four or five 78’s in it, and there’d be Fats Waller and Art Tatum, and people like that, Artie Shaw, you know, all of the famous guys at the time. And I got kind of attracted to that. I said, like they’d put them on the record player and I’d rock, like I’m rocking now, I rocked so much in my crib upstairs in my bedroom that I actually (and I’ve got the scar to this day) rocked my crib into the hallway and the whole crib came right down the stairs and my mother and father thought I was dead. But one of the scars is © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

there, I’ll tell you about the other one which I got later on. But I was always rocking. I just always loved to rock. Even in a car, even in a straight chair I rock. I don’t know why but I do. But the music was always in the house. And my uncle was a bass player, my grandfather — who lived to be 100 — was a violin player and a shoemaker, and his wife, my grandmother, my father’s mother, was a pianist — not a jazz pianist but a pianist, and they played the theater circuit with this fascination of a 4-year-old drummer, and they ended up playing the Hippodrome Theater in New York City with Baby Rose Marie, who was later on I believe “The Dick Van Dyke Show,” Rose Marie. And she was on the bill as well in the Hippodrome Theater. So that was the way that started. But my fascination came from the musical part of my family.
Was the — are you Italian?
I’m 3/4 Italian, 1/4 Irish. My grandmother, the pianist, was born in Ireland. That’s a nice combination.
No kidding.
And the other three are Italians.
I just wondered, you know, the Italians often have a musical heritage, with the mandolins and all that.
Well he was a violinist, and baritone horn player too. My grandfather.
Do you recall if the music that you were getting into, were your parents using the word “jazz” or was it just the music that was in the house?

Well I mean first of all I was 4 years old when it started so I don’t know if it was swing or big band. I can’t really recall the word “jazz” until later on. We moved to Buffalo in 1949, and that’s when the jazz started to come into play. But I mean as I would call it, it was like the big band era, the swing era you know, like Benny Goodman and all of that. The jukeboxes would be loaded with that kind of music. “Stardust,” and “I Can’t Get Started With You,” and “Begin the Beguine” with Artie Shaw, and all of that stuff.
So by the time you were in like junior high school, had you decided on your career path so to speak?

Well we can start a little bit earlier than that. When we moved to Buffalo my father decided I was going to be a piano player. And I took piano lessons. And we lived in downtown Buffalo for a couple of years, and I started learning out of the Thompson method. And then in 1952 we moved to Cheektowaga, New York, which is a suburb of Buffalo, and every time we moved I’d have to change piano teachers, and that piano teacher would start me over with their method. So like I was becoming very disenchanted. You know like okay I got to this point, but no, I want to start you the way I teach so then we’d start over. Then we moved here, to Cortland, in 1953, and I started again on the piano. By this time I was becoming very disenchanted, although I wish I had © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

stuck with it because it sure was a lot easier to play an acoustic piano than it was to lug that stuff around. So anyway, that thing kind of fizzled out. Then I took up the trumpet. That lasted for a couple of years, right up here at Parker School, a couple of blocks away. And that was okay but that didn’t work out either. And in 1956 Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey, the Dorsey Brothers Orchestra, came to Cortland. You went by it on your way here, it’s a place called Skateland. It was a roller skating rink. Now it’s just a vacant building. It became Grossman’s Lumber and it’s just a building up there. Well we went in that summer, and I still hadn’t focused on — my father just said, “he hasn’t got it, he just doesn’t have it man, you know I mean he’s not going to be a musician.” Because I had dropped two instruments.
But he wanted you to be.

Well he wanted me to be exposed to music. I’m not sure he wanted it to go quite the way it went, as you will find out later in the interview. But I walked into that thing, it was July of 1956. And at that time Jackie Gleason was big, but he would have a summer replacement and it was Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey. In fact, that summer replacement — one of the episodes of the summer replacement was when the juggler was on the show of the Dorsey Brothers, when Charlie Parker was watching it, as he died. In fact in the movie you see the juggler and in the scene when he’s in the Stanhope Hotel with the Baroness de Koenigswarter, they used the actual scene. Well that summer they also went on the road. So anyway I walked in there, and the drummer was Louis Bellson. He was married to Pearl Bailey. And she was in an automobile sitting behind the place, she didn’t come in. But he drove separately from the band. And he did a drum solo — now I’m not a hundred percent sure it was “Skin Deep,” because that was what he did with Duke Ellington. But, since it was his arrangement and I’m sure he owned the rights to it, it very well could have been “Skin Deep.” I just know that it was pretty deep. And I watched it. And Charlie Shavers was playing trumpet, Lee Castle was in the trumpet section, which is neither here nor there, Frank Maynes, and then they broke down to the — I think they call it the Clambake Seven when they went to a Dixieland band. But the band was ferocious man, absolutely ferocious. And Louie Bellson was ferocious. So I said to my father, I said, “why don’t I try the drums?” So we went down to a local music store. And he wasn’t going to buy me a set of drums, because he had seen me lose interest in the other things. So we bought a practice pad, a pair of drum sticks, and Duke Ellington’s “Ellington Uptown,” which featured Louis Bellson playing “Skin Deep.” Well from then on it was pretty much drums for me.
Louie Bellson was with the Dorsey Brothers after Ellington?

Yes. That record, that “Ellington Uptown” I believe was in ’52 or ‘3, and they came here in ’56. It was July of ’56. For Christmas that year — I had never touched the drums up © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

until this point. I had a practice pad and I wrecked pillows and, you know, I was ruining the furniture playing along with it. I think I had a cardboard drum or like one of those things kids get. They’re not going to last long, especially if you’re trying to play “Skin Deep,” which I mean I never could play that anyway. But the thing is that that whole bit, like that Christmas I got a snare drum, a 26” bass drum and one steel cymbal. And it was steel, it was not brass or anything. I’ve never seen one like it before or since. I gave it to somebody else just as a thing. But he wasn’t even going to give me a hi-hat stand yet. He said — see he played piano and he had an organo attachment, which is a thing you may or may not be familiar with, but you used to put things underneath the piano keys and this big amplifier on the side made it sound like an organ and you’d control the volume with the thing that came out and you’d move your legs. So he would play all the left hand, and he was a very strict timekeeper anyway.
It was called a what?

An organo — O-R-G-A-N-O. It’s a great big amp, and you had to have them come and put all the things underneath the piano keys, and then you’d turn the thing on and then it had little things — so it made it like an organ sound and he played the bass and I’d be playing along with it. But he was so strict on me. And he was playing with Spiegle Willcox’s band at the time. And Spiegle and the guys — in other words I got this thing and as the time went on, that spring, he would bring the guys in and I would improve. I mean they started coming in when I had the pad, just come in and have a drink before going to a job. And he would criticize me pretty bad. I mean it was kind of embarrassing actually. Because if I screwed up the time or overplayed a drum break, I mean he’d say, “you overplayed that break.” Then they’d all get in the car and drive off to the job and leave me alone with my muse you know. And I would feel sad about it. You know, but it wasn’t like he was being mean it was just a straight fact. But my first job came in July of 1957. A wedding reception. And I had — you’re looking at a guy right now who is 69 years old, and you’re looking also at a guy who’s never worked a day in his life, ever. Now the Army was considered training. I mean I did Basic Training then went into Army bands. But I mean I don’t consider that working, that’s training. So I played my first job, I made nine dollars. I shared a paper route with another guy once, a half a paper route, so I did have a half a paper route. Wouldn’t take a full one. Working was just not in my comfort zone once I made that nine dollars for three hours. I said that’s it, rather than getting 50 cents to mow or rake a lawn.
I know exactly what you’re saying.
I’m not sure that this is the best information for students who may be watching. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

I agree. I mean I made four dollars on my first gig. But I made 35 dollars on my first New Year’s Eve gig when I was still in high school and I said, “oh my God.” But I think it’s interesting that your father said, “you overplayed that break.”

Like in other words, at the end of the tune — the LP was coming in at that time. Between 1949 — I think Columbia was the originator of the long playing record. They used to be on ten inches. But there was two records that I remember particularly on that table when we moved to Cortland here, was Harry James’ “One Night Stand,” and he had a drummer named Jackie Mills who absolutely floored me. But what was even more impressive, or as impressive, was a Ted Heath record called “Live at the London Palladium” and the drummer was Ronnie Verrell. And to this day when I play that record I get excited. I mean Ronnie Verrell, he was a devotee — his main inspiration was Don Lamond. And he played those Don Lamond breaks like — abstract breaks but man. That band was on fire. And I would be listening to that, and then the Salt City Five was a Dixieland band that had won the Arthur Godfrey Show, and that was one of the records on the table, and I wore the cushions on the couch out playing along to that with a drummer named Bob Cousins — and I later went with the Salt City Six, and finally got to meet Bob Cousins and actually played bass with him, because I play the bass as well — not as well, I mean in addition to the drums. And I actually got to play with one of my idols, was him. And then well we can continue on with the Don Lamond, Jake Hanna and that thing. But that’s where that went. But then if you want to go — I’ll let you ask the questions.

Yeah. Were you developing, by the time you were in your teens and so forth, any kind of personal filter — oh I really want to play this kind of music and I don’t care for this kind of music too much. Or was it just like a gig is a gig?

No it wasn’t quite like that. You see because of what I told you was on that table, there was the Salt City Five, which was Dixieland, then Eddie Condon’s music called “Jam Session Coast to Coast,” which had the Rampart Street Paraders on one side with Nick Fatool, a great drummer, and on the other side was the Condon band, which was just dynamite, with Wild Bill Davison and all those guys. And then there was a big band. So like I was in between — and like Ellington “Uptown” and I was right in between. So I had to learn — I learned all of these Dixieland songs, because Spiegle’s band was coming out of that thing. Because he had played with Bix Beiderbecke in the Jean Goldkette Orchestra. So I pretty much came out of the direction of big band to small groups, to like we would play — another record that was on the table was the soundtrack from “The Benny Goodman Story.” Now here I’m listening to Gene Krupa play “Sing Sing Sing” and I’m playing it on the floor and I’m keeping my father awake as he’s taking a nap getting ready to go to a gig. He said, “you’ve got to stop, I’m taking a nap.” But on one side of that was the Benny Goodman Trio playing “China Boy” and “Avalon” — the © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
quartet was with Hamp. So I started playing that music. So I mean it was all subsumed. It was subsumed as just being jazz.

That’s so interesting, because I had the same experience with the soundtrack from the Glenn Miller movie. A big band, and there were some Louis Armstrong cuts on the other side because he was in the movie.

It’s funny you would say that because Moe Purtill, the original drummer with the Glenn Miller band, who is on that, sat right here and played drums. He came with a friend of mine and my father played piano over there, I played the bass, and Moe was right there. What a thrill. I mean I met Moe and we became good friends. He was one of my heroes too because one Christmas I got that little deluxe edition 45s of the Glenn Miller edition with Moe Purtill and that was one of the records that I had when I got that set of drums. I didn’t even know how to tune a set of drums, because it was calfskin heads in those days. I didn’t know if you’re supposed to loosen them up on hot summer days. One day I woke up in the morning and all my drum heads were split because the sun was beating down on them and they tightened up. I said, “who’s been playing my drums.” They went, “nobody, they’ve just been sitting in the sun.”
Okay. So do you remember what kind of music, some of the songs you would have played at your first wedding gig?

Well I mean it would have been “It Had to be You,” — oh what were the songs — “Poor Butterfly.” Of the songs — the standards of 1956. I mean we weren’t playing Patti Page’s “Love” or whatever, “Love Love Love.” We weren’t doing that kind of stuff. We were doing “Someday Sweetheart,” “Charmaine,” “I Found a New Baby.” Things like that. But usually at weddings you couldn’t really unload because dancers, you know, they’ve got to do the — now I’ve got to play a waltz, for the wedding waltz or whatever it was, things like that. So I had to learn that. I had to learn how to play a cha-cha. You know, the bossa novas weren’t in yet so at least I was spared that. I’m not a big cha-cha fan and I don’t even like bossa novas to be honest with you. You can edit that out.
That’s okay. Hey you don’t have to like everything. Well it seems like you must have been getting to a point where you decided well this is what I’m going to do.

Well as I said, well okay, between my junior and senior year of high school of course I discovered the joys of physical relationships with women along that period of time. And my girlfriend at the time happened to be the prettiest girl in the school. But I had played, at the age of 15, now I had gotten mononucleosis and had to stay home for two weeks. Mono is a blood — they call it “kissing disease” actually. So anyway, as soon as I got released from that I’m going back to school and Arnie Koch from — they’re reforming the Salt City Six up on Memory Lane up in Syracuse. Jack Maheu, Will Alger, trumpet player Paul Squire, my father on piano — because I had sat in with the Salt City Six prior © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

to that, when I was 14. But let me preface that by saying that because my eyes were bad at that time we used to go to New York. And we’d go to the Taft Hotel when Vincent Lopez’s band was playing. Because my father — we would stay at the Taft and they used to have a thing called “Shake the Maracas” contest, which was a radio show. And they had me sit in on drums at 14. I’ve got photos of it. And man I was more nervous than a prostitute in church. Or you could say a whore in church. But you can edit that too. So anyway, I sat in. So every time we went there I sat in with them. Then he would take me down to Nick’s to hear either Billy Maxted’s band or whatever band was in Nick’s. And then we’d end the evening — we’d go to Birdland of course, but we’ll get to that a little later — and the Hickory House went to four in the morning so I’d go and hear Marian McPartland’s trio.
Joe Morello?

No Joe was gone by then. But the drummer that I did see there was Jake Hanna. And that was my first meeting with Jake. But let’s see, okay, so anyway, let’s get back to when I was 15, during that summer break, I had played with the band, okay, in the fall, at age 15 I had been released from my medical restrictions because of the mononucleosis, to go back to school. The phone rings and now they want me to play at Memory Lane with the Salt City Six. And now this job went on, they used to go from nine to one or nine to two in those days. I of course never made school on Monday morning. And here I am now playing, and I wasn’t even legally allowed to in those days, because you’re not supposed to be playing in gin mills. That was a law. But I looked a little old for my age, like I do now. But one time my homeroom teacher came in and he says, “now I know why you’re never at school on Monday mornings.” He said, “that’s all right I like jazz, I’ll cover for you.” But anyway, so that summer they called and they said, “we want you to go on the road with us permanently, we’re going on the road.” So that was a decision. My mother was, “oh no you can’t, no you’re not going on the road at age 16” or whatever it was. And I was begging. I says, “man, I’m not mowing lawns, I’m not doing anything, I’m not playing Friday nights.” I didn’t play with the school dance band because why play for 3 dollars at the YMCA when I could be making 15 — well it was 12 to 15 to 18 dollars with my father’s band or Spiegle’s band, or whatever band. Anyway my father said, he said, “okay we’re going to let him go but we’re going to put him in charge of Jack Maheu and Will Alger, that they’ll watch out for him.” That was like letting the hen guard — the fox guarding the henhouse. These guys, man I was loaded constantly with these guys. Now they’re going to Pennsylvania to play at the Penn Sheraton and the legal drinking age is 21 there. Now 18 here. See that means it’s all changed in New York State as you know. So we’d go to after-hours clubs and we’d be playing liar’s poker and I’d be getting — and then of course I came home in the fall and had to go back to school for my senior © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

year. That was between my junior and senior year. And I played with the high school band all of that time. I had actually, to back it up a little bit, from Parker School up the street, for disciplinary reasons, I was sent to St. Mary’s School which is right about seven houses that way. They didn’t have a band. So they figured — so here I am not really learning how to read music as well as I’d like to have, and Burton Stanley was a professor up at Potsdam, was the band director there. And he played a job with a big band up in Syracuse with Spiegle, up at Hotel Syracuse. I sat in and he said to my father, “you’ve got to let me have him. You’ve got to send him to the high school.” Well I was asked, delicately asked, to leave St. Mary’s School for disciplinary reasons once again. Not like kids today carrying guns to school, but just a troublemaker you know, or whatever, talking back, that kind of thing. So I get to the high school and I went right to Burton Stanley and the high school band director and I said, “Prof,” we called him Prof Stanley. Corky Fabrizio took his place because he went up to Potsdam. And I said, “Prof, you’d better put me in the junior band.” I said, “my eyes, I’m not going to be able to read this music in senior band.” He said, “let me worry about that.” He said, “your eyes will catch up to your hands, don’t worry.”
Do you mean your eyesight?
No. My reading. Yeah. “Your eyes will catch up to your hands.”
Okay. I didn’t quite understand, if your eyesight was bad.

No I mean it’s like “nice eyes baby” you know, in other words like you can read real well. And it didn’t take too long. I was always hoping for a sunny day during marching band season because then we’d go outside and be practicing marching band stuff, which was no problem. But on rainy days we had to go into symphonic or concert band and oh man, that was, for me, I just didn’t enjoy that.
Did your fellow, if you had friends that were musicians, were they jealous or were they enthralled by your quote road gigs and stuff? Or were they aware that you were doing that?
Well are you talking during the high school years?
I’m talking of high school, yeah.

I was just gone. I mean I think a couple of them thought that my girlfriend might be available which wasn’t the case. But I guess so. I guess they could have been jealous. But they — see I was into the jazz thing. And they were into Buddy Holly and that kind of a thing. I mean Ronnie Dio was from Cortland. I mean Ronnie Padavona, but he went with Ronnie Dio. I don’t know if you remember him with Black Sabbath? He passed away a couple of years ago. And there were several famous musicians from Cortland. I mean Ray Crisara played with Toscanini. And there was Arnold Gabriel had the Air Force Band for like 30 years. He was the conductor of that. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
What’s his name?

Arnold Gabriel. It was funny, like Toscanini’s son, his father was Frank Crisara. And they had the Old Timer’s Band here in Cortland. And all those musicians, they still have it but it’s not the Old Timers, I mean they’re all gone. They were old timers when I was — 50 years ago they were old timers. They still call it the Old Timers Band. I guess guys like me are in it, but I don’t play in it. So he comes home from playing with Toscanini and they’re having a rehearsal. And Frank Crisara, a handlebar moustache guy like this, and although the trumpet player’s naturally going to give the lead trumpet part to his son, Ray Crisara, who I think is still alive teaching school in Austin, Texas. Fantastic trumpet player. Fantastic. And he had the Italian accent, because I used to live — so he starts playing whatever it is, and he looks back and he sees that his son is playing the solo cornet — or solo trumpet, first trumpet — solo cornet it was. He said, “what the hell is goin’ on around here?” He says, “dees guys they come here every week over hea.” He says, “maybe you play first chair with Toscanin, you play last chair with me.” And here Bob Britano and all these guys said fine. But he was one of the famous guys from Cortland. There’s been a few of them from here.
You know you mentioned Buddy Holly, and that era of rock & roll. When I listen to that music, in fact I play a lot of it now, a lot of it’s basically swing music.
Actually it is.
Right? “Rock Around the Clock” is a swing song.
Um hum. It doesn’t have an eight beat feel.
Right that music didn’t —

I didn’t want to be — I mean rhythm & blues was nice, you know, Louis Jordan and the Tympani Five. That was something that was sitting on the dining room table. I can’t remember all the names of the tunes, I’ve still got them there. But I mean that was Earl Bostic, all of those were swing music. But when it went into eight beat, when it started becoming [scats] that’s when I kind of lost interest in it.
Can I ask you about — I don’t think I’ve heard that term in a long time, “eight beat.”
Well eight beat meaning straight eighths as opposed to like a shuffle or a ding-ding-ka- ding, where the right hand’s playing eighth notes.
Okay, even up and down eighth notes.

Right. And I like to play that kind of music because that freed me up, which a lot of guys didn’t. See a lot of guys, a lot of the swing players played four on the floor. Even though Blakey feathers the bass drum and all of those guys, and so do I. But it’s not like a pounding four on the floor. We call it four on the floor. But I like to — once I started hearing some guys dropping bombs, that’s when I said now that frees me up to like not be necessarily — because once the bass amps came in, the timekeeper in the band is the bass © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

player, really. You know. He’s the one that’s laying the time down. And I’m there to shade and color. Somebody’ll say, “well it’s dragging” or “it’s rushing.” I mean yeah, you can put an edge on the beat or put it behind the beat or whatever. I mean I’ve got a Miles’ Davis record, “Miles at the Black Hawk” when they start “Bye Bye Blackbird” at a certain tempo, and it’s almost a ballad by the time it ends. But it’s swinging all the way down.
Swinging all the way down. Yow.
Yeah but to just sit there like [scats]. You know I like to [scats] you know, like break it up a little bit.
I think that’s very interesting what you just said about the bass player.
Yeah, they’re the timekeeper.
I agree.

Especially when amps came in. Now when they were just back there and they couldn’t be heard, you know, they had to have the strings a lot higher off the fingerboard because they had to pull harder. But now they’ve got the amp, let the amp do the work, I can put the thing down and the facility’s more there, and it changed.
So what happens if the bass player starts being looser with the time, and you are too, and the drummer is too.
Well when you say looser with the time, are you thinking of Bill Evans with Scott LaFaro?
I guess, or, I guess just bass players who want to be more involved —
In interplay with the — okay.
Yeah.

Okay well that was when Scott LaFaro came into the game, and Bill Evans, and that’s when things started to change. But at that point the music was changing and, but it didn’t mean that you didn’t have to have that metronome in your head. You still had to know where it was. But everybody had to know then. It wasn’t somebody sitting there with a metronome keeping track of it. You know, I mean it was in your head at that point.
What was the first bop record that you heard, or did you hear bop live first. How did it sort of enter?

The first bop record I ever heard was with my father when we went over to Oneonta, New York. In those days they used to have speakers outside of the music store playing the latest things, you know, that kind of thing. And we went in there, and I’ve still got the original 78. It was “One Bass Hit” by Dizzy Gillespie. And on one side was the big band version and on the other side was the small band version. And I’ve still got that 78. And I said, now that got my attention. That did get my attention. And that was the first one. But that would have been in the early 50’s as well and I hadn’t even started drums yet. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Did you start leaning towards that kind of music, to play bop or hard hop?
Well, as I said earlier, we used to go to New York to go to a certain optician — let me see is it optician or —
Is it an optometrist?

No it’s the guy that is a doctor. It’s an optician, isn’t it? Not an optometrist. Not the guy that makes the glasses, no, this is an optician. And as I’d say we’d go, and I was starting to get into listening to the bebop pretty good then. Although we would always go to Nick’s, we’d always go to Condon’s, we went to the Metropole one day and we sat there for eight hours listening to Coleman Hawkins and Charlie Shavers and Mickey Sheen was a great drummer then too. He’s since passed away. And I was in awe. And then they had two bands. The other band was Cozy Cole with Roy Eldridge and certain guys like that, which was amazing too.
